attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter. He states them as his rebuttal, not as a quote.

semantics.note: The firm clause 'they haven't' is an observation. The proposition also includes the hedged 'no path' clause, but the contract rightly scores only the firm part.

contract.note: Reading 'costs' as the unit cost of using the models fits the hype claim he is answering and his later line that AI 'isn't getting much more efficient'. It is a fair, ordinary reading. A total-spend reading would flip the result, and the contract flags this.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own Nov 2023 price list: GPT-4 Turbo is 2-3x cheaper per token than GPT-4, inside the period. A company's own list prices are the direct record of its prices.
May 2024: GPT-4o matches GPT-4 Turbo on English text and code at 50% lower API price, before the post date.
Independent Epoch analysis (2025, before the cutoff) finds prices falling at fixed capability. It does not attribute the falls to thinner margins. This supports price as a proxy for cost.
Covers training costs per model, a different metric from unit cost of use. Relevant only to the other reading of 'costs'.

reviews.rationale: On the contract's fair plain reading, per-token prices for GPT-4-class output fell by several times between Mar 2023 and Jul 2024 (e1, e2). That contradicts 'they haven't' come down. Rising training spend (e4) is a different metric. Using prices as a stand-in for internal costs is a known limit, and e3 eases it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, stated as his rebuttal of the job-creation hype.

semantics.note: A firm past-tense observation covering about 18 months. The normalised proposition matches it.

contract.note: Read literally as zero jobs, the claim is trivially false. In context he means job creation at economy scale, so the 'meaningful' plain reading is fair and ordinary. It sets no threshold, which leaves the evidence short of settling it.

evidence.note: GenAI-related postings grew 30-fold but are only about 0.11% of US postings. These are gross postings, not net new jobs, so they neither meet nor clearly fail a 'meaningful' test.
Indeed economists say GenAI is already creating jobs. This cuts against the literal wording, but they give no net, economy-wide figure.
About 1,200 staff at OpenAI is gross hiring at one firm. That is too small to count as economy-wide creation under the plain reading.

reviews.rationale: Some GenAI-related jobs clearly existed (e1-e3). But no source in the packet measures net new jobs caused by GenAI across the economy, and the plain reading sets no threshold. The evidence available does not settle whether job creation was 'meaningful'.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: An observation hedged with 'don't even seem capable'. The hedge is kept. 'Innovations' may be broader than restaurant ordering AI, but the proposition offers that only as an example.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats the claim as hedged, with no measure of job replacement, and does not score it.

reviews.rationale: The claim is an impression hedged with 'seem', and he gives no measure of what replacing jobs means. Under policy, hedged wording is not scored. No evidence is needed, and the empty packet does not break the case.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' forecast. 'Most likely' hedges only which provider is hit, and that is kept. The proposition assumes a collapse, and the contract treats the collapse as part of the forecast.

contract.note: Requiring a recognised bubble collapse before scoring is faithful to 'part of the collapse'. No deadline was given, so the claim cannot fail on time. The early-resolution rule is fair.

evidence.note: Jan 2026: Microsoft shares fell 10% and a shareholder suit followed. This is investor punishment linked to AI spending, but it did not come with a bubble collapse.
The June 2026 suit targets disclosure of Microsoft's AI infrastructure spending. This is dissent, but no collapse is shown.
Confirms the size of the Jan 2026 drop. Microsoft was still worth about $3.2T afterwards, so this was a sell-off, not a collapse.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and the packet shows no recognised collapse of the generative AI bubble by 2026-10-28. Microsoft's sell-off and lawsuit match the predicted kind of punishment, but without a collapse the early-resolution rule is not met. Later October sell-offs were correctly left out.
